data.title: Investors' recent money moves show a preference for lowering risks over boosting rewards
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Investors have been steadily pouring more money into 'quality' companies than 'momentum' stocks

The AI buildout is not the only thing investors cite as they move toward quality, according to Rene Reyna, Invesco's head of equity ETF strategy.

In a sign that investors are feeling anxious about the outlook for the stock market, they have recently shown a clear preference for "quality" shares, which tend to fare best during periods of broad market declines, over the previously highflying momentum stocks.

The S&P 500 is weighted by companies' market value, which means shares of companies with higher market capitalizations have more influence than those with lower market caps. There are various ways to invest along with the index or to try to outperform it by applying factors to hold subsets of the S&P 500.

If you hold shares of the $818 billion State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY, an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 SPX by holding all of its stocks, you can see how technology stalwarts and rapid growers dominate. The top five holdings of SPY - Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN) and two common-share classes of Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) - make up 30.6% of the portfolio.

There are various exchange-traded funds that include S&P 500 stocks but have different risk profiles, including the lower-risk $99 billion Invesco Equal Weight S&P 500 Index ETF RSP, in which each component is weighted the same, the even-lower-risk $19 billion Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF SPHQ, and the more aggressive $22 billion Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF SPMO.

Rene Reyna, Invesco's head of equity ETF strategy, told MarketWatch that flows of new money into the quality ETF (SPHQ) have been steady for most of this year, with positive flows every month except for August. That month, $680 million flowed out of SPHQ, while $714 million flowed into the momentum ETF (SPMO). But in September, the action was subdued and in the opposite direction, with $3.4 million flowing into SPHQ and $43 million flowing out of SPMO. (See below for what constitutes quality and momentum.)

What might make the quality approach work, for now

During the first half of 2026, the equal-weighted approach fared well, with RSP returning 12%, while the S&P 500 returned 10.2%. But SPHQ did even better with a first-half return of 20.8%, while SPMO shined with a 36% return.

SPHQ holds the 100 stocks among the S&P 500 that rank highest according to a quality score that combines returns on equity, debt-to-book value and an "accruals ratio" of operating assets to total assets. The index tracked by this fund is rebalanced twice a year. Each stock is weighted by the product of its quality score and its market capitalization.

SPMO holds the 100 stocks of companies in the S&P 500 with the highest "momentum scores." Twice a year, the components of the S&P 500 are ranked by how much their prices have risen over the previous 12 months, then scored to take volatility into account. The portfolio is made up of the 20% of companies in the S&P 500 that score highest, which are then weighted by a combination of the momentum score and market capitalization

Here's the latest year-to-date performance chart for the three ETFs and the full S&P 500:

The Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF has underperformed the S&P 500 so far this year. The Invesco Momentum ETF tends to outperform the full index during bull markets, but it can underperform during down periods for the broad market.

The chart shows that SPMO has experienced quite a bit of volatility this year, with prices coming down significantly since June 30.

Longer term, SPMO has been a stellar performer, with a five-year return of 137%, against 83% for the S&P 500 and 75% for SPHQ.

But according to Reyna, SPHQ is the safer play for investors during periods of souring sentiment. When asked how SPHQ might help investors who are questioning whether or not the trillions of dollars being spent on the build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure will eventually be justified through profits, he said that based on meetings with clients, "the challenge appears to be beyond AI."

He said that prior to the latest U.S. consumer-price index report, which showed inflation at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.7%, "we were looking at a low probability for another rate increase" when the Federal Reserve meets next week.

And Reyna said investors were also watching 10-year U.S. Treasury notes BX:TMUBMUSD10Y, which were yielding 5.02% early on Thursday. He said a 6% 10-year yield would represent a "challenge" to investors, who "might want to take a 6% return rather than the risk in the stock market."

When compared with the S&P 500's price movement, SPMO has had 142.48% upside capture over the past year, with 106.4% downside capture, according to Reyna. Meanwhile, SPHQ has had 86.05% upside capture, with only 61.1% downside capture. Basically, you might not make as much with quality relative to momentum when the market is rising, but you also lose a lot less when the market falls.

For investors who wish to stay invested while softening the effect of a possible market correction, the lower-volatility approach has been gaining in popularity.

-Philip van Doorn

data.title: My niece's college rent is covered by a 529 plan. What else can I pay for tax-free?
data.description:
By Jillian Berman

'We worked out a monthly budget of $1,500 for her share of rent, utilities and food, including groceries and meals on campus'

"Last spring, the university emailed me its estimated 2025-2026 cost of attendance for a full-time student living off campus: $16,000." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Extra Credit,

I'm thinking ahead to my 2026 Form 1040 tax filing and have a question about documenting qualified 529 plan expenses.

I set up a 529 plan for my niece when she was born. She started college about a year ago, and scholarships and financial aid covered about half of her tuition, plus room and board. I covered the other half. She was considering moving into an apartment for her sophomore year, and I had to work through complications about leases, providing an allowance and related expenses.

She is now a sophomore engineering student and has rented a house near campus with four friends. We worked out a monthly budget of $1,500 for her share of rent, utilities and food, including groceries and meals on campus. That seemed reasonable based on the overall costs, assuming roughly a 50/50 split between eating at home and on campus.

We're two months into the arrangement and, so far, everything is going well. She has been responsible, and the budget seems to be working. My question is about record-keeping for the qualified expense breakdown for her 529 plan. Last year, it was pretty straightforward because she lived in a dorm, and the university provided the expense breakdown.

Last spring, the university emailed me its estimated 2025-2026 cost of attendance for a full-time student living off campus: $16,000, or $8,000 per semester. The academic year is nine months long, so her budget of $1,500 per month comes to $13,500 for the school year, or $6,750 per semester. I'd appreciate any guidance or suggestions from those who have navigated this before.

Am I correct in understanding that, for purposes of using 529 funds for room and board, I can use the university's published off-campus cost-of-attendance allowance as the limit, provided her actual expenses are at least that amount? Do I need to keep detailed records of every expense, or would the university's published allowance and proof of rent and utility payments generally be sufficient? Are receipts required for groceries and meals purchased on campus?

The Aunt

If you have questions about student loans, college or debt, email Extra Credit at jberman@marketwatch.com

Dear Aunt,

How lucky your niece is to have someone like you to help support her in college. It can be challenging for many families to find the funds to put away for college. Roughly 40% of families with children use college savings accounts, and the average balance in accounts for children when they're 18 is about $41,000, according to ISS Market Intelligence.

That's enough to cover a few years of tuition and fees at public universities in the state, on average, but too little to pay for one year of tuition and fees at a nonprofit private college on average, leaving not much room to pay for the kind of expenses you're able to cover for your niece.

Now, to your question. Mark Kantrowitz, a college savings expert, advises you to document your expenses to make sure they are qualified.

He suggests saving copies of a lease agreement and any evidence you actually paid the rent, like a receipt or cancelled check. Your niece should also hang on to utility bills and receipts from the grocery store and meals out. Be aware that the Internal Revenue Service expects taxpayers to be able to substantiate any qualified expenses.

If keeping track of so many expenses the old-fashioned way seems complicated, Mary Morris, the CEO of Commonwealth Savers, Virginia's 529 plan, suggests using a prepaid card. Every month, you can load money that was disbursed from the 529 onto the card and instruct your niece only to use it for qualified expenses, like rent and food. That way you'll have a record of how the 529 money was spent.

For purchases that don't qualify, like concert tickets, your niece should use a separate credit card or debit card tied to a bank account.

Morris suggests explaining this card system to your niece and then checking in at regular intervals to make sure she's following the rules.

Keep receipts

Both Kantrowitz and Morris agree that having your niece get into the habit of record-keeping is not only useful for tax purposes, but can also help her practice the kind of organization and financial responsibility that she'll need once she graduates.

There are a few extra things you - and others who are paying for college - should keep in mind when using 529 funds.

First, it appears you're already aware of the first one - making sure you know the school's cost of attendance and not spending any 529 money beyond that amount or else the expense won't qualify.

Second, you can only use 529 money for room and board if your student is attending college at least half of the time.

Third, you can't double dip the 529 and tax credits, so if you're receiving the American Opportunity Tax Credit for qualified education expenses, for example, subtract the amount you're getting in tax credits from the cost of attendance and only spend the remainder from your 529 money. The $2,500-per-student credit covers tuition fees and course materials for undergraduates, but it does not cover room-and-board costs or other personal expenses.

Finally, save any tax forms the college gives you like the 1098-T, which documents tuition expenses, so you'll have them at tax time.

Ultimately, though, you're already on the right track, both because you've socked away enough so that your niece doesn't have to borrow or rely on her own funds to pay for expenses beyond tuition, and because you're thinking about how to best make sure those expenses are recorded properly.

This experience of receiving the money and working with you to help document her spending will help set up your niece for a solid financial future and help to teach her how to manage a budget as an additional bonus.

-Jillian Berman

data.title: My spouse was awarded $90,000 from my 401(k) in our divorce. How is that fair?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I retired in 2020 and subsequently went through a divorce a few years later'

"Earlier in my career, while I was still working, I went through another divorce. I was able to replenish the funds distributed from my retirement plan on a pretax basis." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I retired in 2020 and subsequently went through a divorce a few years later. As part of the division of assets, approximately $90,000 was awarded to my ex-spouse from my 401(k). Is this normal, and does that kind of arrangement sound fair to you?

Earlier in my career, while I was still working, I went through another divorce. I was able to replenish the funds distributed from my retirement plan on a pretax basis, in addition to making my regular contributions. Is it possible to do something similar now that I am retired?

Happily and Unhappily Divorced

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

Life will be easier for you if you make peace with the outcome.

Dear Divorced,

You hit on something that comes up a lot in divorce: fairness versus acceptance.

The former is adjudicated by the judge in the proceedings. They make their ruling using the letter of the law - evaluating marital property and what the lower-earning spouse contributed to the marriage. In recent weeks, I have received letters from readers who have balked over splitting their retirement funds with an estranged spouse who gave up their career to stay at home, raise their children and run their household - often a job that has no official start or end time. I'm curious to know what percentage of your 401(k) that $90,000 made up.

Ultimately, I leave you to decide whether this $90,000 distribution was fair because you're the one who has to live with the court's decision. Life will be easier for you if you make peace with the outcome; otherwise, every time you decide not to upgrade your flight, not take a vacation or not spend money on a shiny object, you run the risk of harking back to this moment in divorce court when your 401(k) was suddenly $90,000 lighter. Divorce is not just about legal and financial separation; the most challenging part of all is emotional separation and closure.

As Tracy Callahan - co-founder of the Divorce Coaches Academy, an organization that helps people journey through the most painful and challenging parts of the process - points out in this podcast, the hardest part of a divorce agreement is having to live with it. "I think about settlement agreements the same way I think about buying shoes," she says. "When you buy a pair of shoes, you don't buy them because they look good sitting on the shelf. You buy them because you're going to have to walk in them. The same is true with divorce agreements."

Understanding the legal basis for the $90,000 award to your ex-spouse may help. Contributions made to your 401(k) and IRA during a marriage, including returns on the principal, are often considered marital property, unless otherwise stated in a prenuptial agreement. Funds contributed before the marriage, after your legal separation or received as an inheritance are usually regarded as separate property. Equitable-distribution states divide assets equitably, but not necessarily 50/50, while community-property states aim to divide marital property 50/50.

Don't miss: We have a $300,000 mortgage with a 2.75% interest rate. I want to pay it off. My husband says I'm crazy. Who's right?

Limits and rules for 401(k)s

These instructions from the Internal Revenue Service sum it up: "If a plan participant gets divorced, his or her ex-spouse may become entitled to a portion of the participant's retirement-account balance. Depending on the type of plan and the amount of benefits, the ex-spouse may have immediate access to his or her portion of those assets or at some point in the future (usually upon the participant's retirement or death). Most plans require an ex-spouse to file a Qualified Domestic Relations Order with the plan administrator before the plan can pay."

After your divorce, it sounds like you boosted your 401(k) contributions based on the terms of your employer-sponsored plan. But limits apply: In 2026, workers can contribute up to $24,500 a year to a 401(k) from their own paycheck, with pretax and Roth contributions counting toward that limit. If you're 50 or older, you can make an additional $8,000 annual catch-up contribution ($32,500 in total), and workers ages 60 to 63 can get an annual $11,250 catch-up ($35,750 in total). Employee and employer contributions can reach $72,000, excluding any catch-ups.

You can usually only contribute to a 401(k) while you are still working. You can, however, rollover your money from your 401(k) to an IRA. People do this to simplify their retirement portfolio, so all their investments are in one place, and also to access a broader range of investments in an IRA. When you roll over money from your 401(k) into an IRA, you won't pay taxes on the rollover itself, but you will pay income taxes when you eventually draw down money from your IRA in retirement - so your investments continue to grow tax-deferred in the meantime.

Vanguard highlights some things to consider before a rollover. "While IRAs can have low fees, your employer-plan fees may be even lower," it says. "You should review your plan's fee structure and the IRA fee structure to determine which might be the most cost-effective. Some 401(k) plans offer institutional shares, which could have lower expense ratios than those of funds typically held in an IRA. If you leave your employer between ages 55 and 591/2, you may take penalty-free withdrawals from your 401(k). IRAs require that you wait until age 591/2."

I wish you a prosperous and resentment-free retirement as you navigate life as a single man.

Related: My father-in-law, 81, sold his $75,000 home to pay his daughter's $50,000 debt. How can I keep him from becoming destitute?

By emailing your questions to The Moneyist or posting your dilemmas on The Moneyist Facebook group, you agree to have them published anonymously on MarketWatch.

My partner of 17 years left me his $1 million home. His children say I influenced him to do so. Should I share my inheritance?

'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life. Is that so bad?

'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, or weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns.

-Quentin Fottrell

data.title: Swanson Vitamins Launches Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro to Champion Registered Dietitians and Licensed Nutritionists at Every Stage of Their Careers
data.description:
Swanson Vitamins Launches Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro to Champion Registered Dietitians and Licensed Nutritionists at Every Stage of Their Careers

Swanson Vitamins Launches Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro to Champion Registered Dietitians and Licensed Nutritionists at Every Stage of Their Careers

PR Newswire

FARGO, N.D., Oct. 24, 2026

New network for health and nutrition professionals offers CPEU-accredited continuing education, profession-wide promotion, practicum support and exam scholarships

FARGO, N.D., Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Swanson Vitamins today launched Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro, a network for health and nutrition professionals. The new initiative champions registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists through every stage of their careers, from students to providers with decades of experience. Created by nutrition professionals for nutrition professionals, Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro offers educational resources, incentives and investments to support practitioners who share Swanson's commitment to uncompromising integrity.

Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro offers tailored resources for both practicing professionals and students. For practicing registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists, the program provides CPEU-accredited continuing education, along with profession-wide promotion of the experts who guide consumers' wellness decisions. For dietetics and nutrition students, Swanson is investing in the next generation of the profession through practicum support and scholarships toward licensing or credentialing exam fees.

As consumers take a more active role in their health, they are increasingly turning to registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists for accurate, science-backed guidance. Through Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro, Swanson aims to help nutrition professionals strengthen their credentials and build expertise in areas where consumers are seeking trusted nutritional support.

"Since 1969, we have been committed to uncompromising integrity in service of everyone's journey to real wellness, and we believe real wellness starts with the experts who guide it," said Erin Del Ponte, EVP Brand Marketing at Swanson Vitamins. "Registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists translate nutrition science into practical, personalized guidance that helps people make informed decisions about their health. With Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro, we are proud to support these professionals at every stage of their careers, from students preparing for their credentialing exams to seasoned providers building expertise in the areas that matter most to consumers today."

Swanson Nexus Pro program highlights

  • CPEU-accredited continuing education for registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists
  • Profession-wide promotion of registered dietitians and licensed nutritionists
  • Practicum support for dietetics and nutrition students
  • Scholarships to help offset licensing or credentialing exam fees

Applications for Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro are open and can be submitted HERE. Additional details, including scholarship award amounts and practicum support details, will be announced in the coming weeks.

Swanson Vitamins Nexus Pro was introduced at the Food & Nutrition Conference & Expo, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics' annual conference, held Oct. 24-27 in San Antonio. This initiative builds on Swanson's longstanding commitment to the nutrition and dietetics community and reflects the company's continued investment in the professionals who help consumers make informed choices on their journey to real wellness.

Media Assets
Photos HERE

About Swanson Vitamins
Since 1969, Swanson Vitamins has offered high-quality, science-backed vitamins and supplements rooted in one simple belief: proof over promise. Nearly six decades before "wellness" became an industry, Swanson was pioneering trustworthy supplement offerings and upholding uncompromising quality standards through intentional sourcing, rigorous in-house and third-party testing and Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP).

Today, Swanson is a Certified GMP Facility recognized by NSF, backed by an in-house team of nutritionists, dietitians, scientists, chemists and pharmacists with a combined 250-plus years of experience. With more than 1,300 products across 36 categories, Swanson doesn't chase trends. It sets standards for integrity, quality and clarity in the supplement industry.

Swanson products are available at SwansonVitamins.com, Amazon and iHerb.com. Learn more at SwansonVitamins.com or follow @swansonvitamins on Instagram.

MEDIA CONTACT
Lauren Torrez, Crowe PR
ltorrez@crowepr.com

data.title: Parabilis Medicines Presents Updated Phase 1/2 Data for Zolucatetide Demonstrating Compelling Efficacy and Favorable Safety and Tolerability Profile in Patients with Desmoid Tumors
data.description:
• Objective response rate of 72.2% among response-evaluable patients receiving a starting dose of ≥450 mg at 32-week landmark
  • Disease control rate of 100% across all response-evaluable patients receiving a starting dose of ≥450 mg, with no disease progression and no treatment discontinuations due to TRAEs
  • Data informed FDA-aligned dose and regimen selection for upcoming PEDESTAL Phase 3 registrational trial, with initiation planned in the first half of 2027 and topline results anticipated in 2029
  • Company to host investor webcast on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 18:00 CEST (12:00 p.m. EDT)

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Oct. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Parabilis Medicines (Nasdaq: PBLS), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company dedicated to creating extraordinary medicines for patients with serious diseases by unlocking historically undruggable targets, today announced updated safety and efficacy data for zolucatetide, the first and only direct inhibitor of the β-catenin:TCF interaction, in patients with desmoid tumors. The data were presented today in an oral presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026, taking place October 23–27, 2026, in Madrid, Spain.

The updated results, based on a June 22, 2026, data cutoff, include data from both the dose escalation and dose optimization portions of the ongoing Phase 1/2 trial and reinforce the strong efficacy and favorable safety and tolerability profile observed with zolucatetide. Among response-evaluable patients who began treatment at a starting dose of ≥450 mg, zolucatetide demonstrated an objective response rate (ORR) of 72.2% (13/18) in a 32-week landmark analysis. A disease control rate (DCR) of 100% was observed across all 46 response-evaluable patients who received a starting dose of ≥450 mg, with no disease progression.

Data from a three-arm randomized dose optimization trial supported selection of a 450 mg weekly induction regimen administered for four cycles, followed by 300 mg every two weeks for long-term maintenance. Following productive end-of-Phase 2 discussions, Parabilis has reached alignment with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on the selected dose and regimen, on the use of a placebo-controlled study design, and on progression-free survival (PFS) as the primary endpoint for registrational development.

Parabilis plans to initiate the randomized, double-blind PEDESTAL Phase 3 trial (Phase 3 Evaluation of DESmoid Tumor Activity with zoLucatetide) in the first half of 2027, with topline results anticipated in 2029.

“Desmoid tumors are chronic and life-altering for patients, often affecting people at a young age, and patients need treatments that can deliver rapid, deep and durable tumor responses with a tolerability profile suited for long-term treatment,” said Mathai Mammen, M.D., Ph.D., Chairman, CEO and President of Parabilis Medicines. “We designed zolucatetide to directly inhibit β-catenin:TCF, a historically undruggable target at the heart of the biology driving these tumors. The depth and consistency of responses we are seeing, together with the favorable safety and tolerability profile observed to date, reinforce our conviction that zolucatetide has the potential to deliver a truly differentiated medicine and meaningfully expand the number of patients who can benefit from treatment. We are very pleased with the clarity of the FDA’s feedback on our registrational development strategy, and with our Phase 3 regimen selected, we are moving with urgency to bring this medicine to patients.”

Updated Phase 1/2 Results
As of the June 22, 2026, data cutoff, 76 patients with desmoid tumors had been enrolled and treated across all dose levels in the dose escalation and dose optimization portions of the trial. Median age was 37 years (range 19–80), and 69.7% of patients were female. The population included both patients who had previously been treated with and failed gamma-secretase inhibitors (GSIs) and patients naive to GSIs.

A total of 48 patients began treatment at a starting induction dose of ≥450 mg, prior to down-dosing for maintenance. Two patients were started at 900 mg, but had an average dose of 400–500 mg over the first four months of treatment. Of these 48 patients, 46 were response-evaluable, and 18 had scans at 32 weeks. Median time on treatment for this cohort was 4.7 months (range 0.5–22.3), reflecting recent enrollment of a substantial portion of the cohort.

Efficacy

  • ORR per RECIST 1.1 was 72.2% (13/18) among all patients evaluable at the 32-week landmark
  • A disease control rate (DCR) of 100% was observed across all 46 response-evaluable patients
  • Responses were observed irrespective of prior gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI) exposure or CTNNB1 or APC mutation status
  • No evidence of disease progression or resistance

Safety

  • Zolucatetide continued to demonstrate a favorable safety and tolerability profile at the selected doses for Phase 3 registrational development
  • Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were predominantly low-grade; the most commonly reported TRAEs were fatigue, alopecia and nausea
  • No patients discontinued treatment due to TRAEs
  • Not associated with ovarian toxicity or high-grade gastrointestinal or skin toxicities commonly reported with GSIs

“The early clinical results with zolucatetide are encouraging, particularly the magnitude and apparent rapidity of tumor responses observed to date,” said Mrinal Gounder, M.D., Sarcoma Medical Oncologist and Early Drug Development Specialist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and presenting author of the study. “Desmoid tumors can impose a substantial physical and emotional burden on patients, and therapies capable of achieving meaningful tumor shrinkage while maintaining acceptable tolerability remain an important clinical goal. These findings support further investigation of zolucatetide in the planned Phase 3 trial.”

The Phase 1/2 trial is ongoing in patients with desmoid tumors and a range of other tumor types driven by alterations in the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and follow-up is continuing. Zolucatetide has received Fast Track and Orphan Drug Designations from the FDA for the treatment of desmoid tumors.

These findings provide further clinical validation of the potential of the Company's Helicon™ platform to unlock disease-driving targets historically considered undruggable.

Investor Webcast
Parabilis will host an investor webcast on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 18:00 CEST (12:00 p.m. EDT) to discuss the updated zolucatetide data that will be presented at ESMO Congress 2026. The webcast will be available on the Investors section of the Parabilis website at https://investors.parabilismed.com. Both the presentation and a replay of the webcast will be available following the event.

About Desmoid Tumors
Desmoid tumors are locally invasive soft-tissue tumors that arise in connective tissues and can be aggressive and recurrent, often causing chronic pain, limited mobility, disfigurement and organ dysfunction. An estimated 30,000 people in the U.S. alone are living with desmoid tumors, including approximately 11,000 who are actively managed, with significant unmet need globally as well. Desmoid tumors typically present in young adults, predominantly females, with many patients requiring prolonged or intermittent treatment. Wnt/β-catenin pathway-activating mutations are the causal driver of desmoid tumors, yet no approved therapies directly target this underlying biology of the disease.

About Zolucatetide
Zolucatetide is an investigational first-in-class and first and only direct inhibitor of the interaction between β-catenin and the T-cell factor (TCF) family of transcription factors, a genetically validated driver of numerous cancers and other serious diseases that has long been considered undruggable. Developed using Parabilis’ Helicon™ peptide platform, zolucatetide is designed to prevent the activation of disease-driving genes by directly targeting β-catenin:TCF, a key downstream node in the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. This approach has the potential to address aberrant Wnt/β-catenin signaling regardless of the upstream APC or β-catenin mutations driving pathway activation, potentially overcoming a key limitation of approaches targeting earlier steps in the pathway.

Zolucatetide is currently being evaluated in an ongoing Phase 1/2 clinical trial (NCT05919264) across a range of indications, including desmoid tumors, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (ACP), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and additional Wnt-driven tumor types.

About Parabilis Medicines
Parabilis Medicines (Nasdaq: PBLS) is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company dedicated to creating extraordinary medicines for patients with serious diseases by unlocking biologically important targets long considered undruggable. The Company has pioneered a new class of alpha-helical peptides – Helicons™ – capable of modulating intracellular proteins that have historically been beyond the reach of conventional medicines. The Company's lead investigational medicine, zolucatetide, is the first and only direct inhibitor of the β-catenin:TCF interaction, a central node in the Wnt/β-catenin pathway that has eluded drug developers for decades. Zolucatetide is being evaluated in the clinic across multiple Wnt/β-catenin-driven diseases, including desmoid tumors, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (ACP), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and a range of other rare and common solid tumor indications. Beyond zolucatetide, Parabilis is pursuing a follow-on β-catenin degrader program and advancing additional Helicon-based programs focused on other challenging targets, including ERG and allosteric ARON in prostate cancer, where we believe our medicines could have life-altering impact. For more information, visit www.parabilismed.com or follow us on LinkedIn.

Forward-Looking Statements

data.title: 'She's living the dream': My stepmother said I can buy my childhood home for $850,000. Is she taking advantage of me?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s'

"She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s. By the time he died, it was worth about $850,000, mostly because it's spacious and in a good neighborhood. He left it to my stepmother, whom he married a few years after my mom died. She is now 74. They were together for 18 years. She took care of him through the whole illness, which I don't take lightly.

Dad told me more than once that the house would be mine someday. My stepmother now wants to sell and move somewhere smaller. She's living the dream in Miami. I offered $700,000. That's $200,000 under market, but I thought it was fair, given that she would skip agent fees and it would be a quick, clean sale. I'd have to stretch to do it, but I could manage.

She was really offended, and she told me as much. She said she's paid the property taxes and the repairs for years (she put a new roof on in 2021). She also said she spent a big chunk of her own savings on my father's care and that the house is basically her retirement plan, and that she can't just hand me $200,000 because I'm sentimental.

Don't miss: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

The $200,000 discount

That's a fair point, and I told her so. What I can't get past is that a few years ago she gave her daughter $200,000 toward a house, and that is how (and why) I came up with the $200,000 haircut on my father's home. I brought that up, and she said things were different then, and pointed out that I have a good job and can buy my own place.

She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died. As my girlfriend at the time said, "Yes, she really went there." That comment really stung. He trusted her with everything, and it feels like his wishes just evaporated. She says she honored him by caring for him and that I'm discounting everything she sacrificed.

I could, of course, walk away and buy somewhere else. I've even looked at a couple of listings. But it wouldn't be the same, and I'd always feel like the house slipped away from our family. I know that my stepsister's place has a sauna in the basement, and I'd bet anything that my stepmother helped pay for that too. Not that I'm keeping score. (OK, I know I am a little.)

Am I being unreasonable?

The Stepson

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

You can't force someone to sell you a house that never legally belonged to you.

Dear Stepson,

Don't allow steam from your stepsister's sauna to cloud your vision. You can grieve the loss of your childhood home without assigning blame.

What's more, you can't force someone to sell you a house that never belonged to you in the first place. Your childhood home, legally and morally, belonged to your father. Even though you grew up there, that doesn't give you the right to a life estate or a $200,000 discount on the purchase price because your stepmother gave her daughter $200,000 toward the down payment on her own home. What's more, selling a house to a family member below fair market value can create a gift of equity equal to the price difference, which the IRS may treat as a taxable gift.

Your late father made a promise that he did not keep, could not keep or decided not to keep. That was his responsibility. It's not your stepmother's job to make good on your father's promises. Whether he made a will leaving her the house or whether she inherited the house through state intestate laws, the end result is the same: She legally owns the house, and she has the right to live there or sell it to whomever she wants.

It is your belief that your father's wishes "evaporated." But wishes, promises and/or intentions evolve, and perhaps he realized that he wanted to take care of his wife of nearly two decades, and die with the knowledge that she would always have a roof over her head. It would have been better to have discussed those plans with you rather than leaving you in a kind of limbo, wondering if he truly wanted to leave his estate to his wife. Chances are, he did.

That does not mean this is an easy or pleasant situation for you. You have an emotional attachment to this property, and you regard your stepmother as an interloper, inheriting a property where your own mother probably once lived. It's a tough break for you and your siblings, if you have any. You made your stepmother an offer and she declined. She may be thinking about her own retirement and financial future.

Don't miss: 'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life. Is that so bad?

Passing judgment

Two decades is a long time to spend with someone. She met your father when she was in her 50s, and she's now rightly concerned about medical costs, if she needs nursing home care, especially if she does not have long-term care insurance, or any other kind of life insurance. This house may be the only asset she has, and downsizing will give her a cushion as she heads towards her 80th birthday in six years. That's quite a reality check.

I'm heartened that you realize that taking care of your father was no small deal for your stepmother. Who will take care of her if she sells you this house for $650,000 and runs out of money? Will you drive her to hospital appointments and spend hours a day with her, making sure that she takes her medication and pays her bills, and has enough to eat? That might sound dramatic, but getting older often comes with health complications.

One could argue that you both "went there." She "went there" by telling you your father wanted her to have his house. You "went there" by using emotional leverage, whether or not you believe it in your heart to be valid, to persuade her to sell this house to you on the cheap. By doing so, you are, whether you realize it or not, also passing judgment on her marriage of 18 years to a man she probably loved very much. You both spoke plainly. That's OK. Just know it's 50/50.

If you want this house, put in an offer when it is listed for sale. If she does get more than one offer and, say, one party offers $50,000 more, she may still decide to sell you the house (and maybe not even mention that she is selling it to you at less than the other offer). Remember, if she gets $950,000 rather than $850,000 - a real possibility if it's a cash buyer and it's a sought-after neighborhood - she would have been giving you a $300,000 discount if she agreed to your proposal.

All is fair in love, second marriages, legal beneficiaries and real estate. Just don't overstretch yourself financially for the sake of nostalgia.

Related: 'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist at qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

'I am a pretty cautious person': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

My sister moved in with our mother, 78, and now says she deserves the $925,000 family home. Is she right?

data.title: AI fever ignites a boom in thematic ETFs as fund managers hunt for their next big hit
data.description:
By Christine Idzelis

It's been a rocky October for the AI trade, putting a dent in big gains so far this year

Robotics ETFs are increasingly coming to the stock market, with AI being a dominant investing theme in 2026.

The runaway success of the artificial-intelligence trade has left investors hungry for the next big market theme. Wall Street fund managers are happily obliging with a flurry of new targeted products, helping investors invest in everything from the rise of robotics to the incipient space economy.

Thematic ETFs are booming in 2026, as asset managers have launched new products at a breakneck pace. The popularity of funds like the Roundhill Memory ETF DRAM, which invests in memory stocks as a subsector of technology and quickly gained traction because they're an important part of the AI trade, has inspired something of a gold rush in the space, as fund companies cast about for the next big hit.

Niche subdivisions of the AI theme have proved particularly popular, as fund managers have launched products tied to everything from AI lab ecosystems to shares of optical companies expected to benefit from the ongoing AI investment boom. Cybersecurity, robotics and defense have been other popular themes.

"AI is the dominant theme," said Bryan Armour, director of ETF and semiliquid fund research at Morningstar, in a phone interview. "What we're seeing in 2026 is product development that refines some of those exposures," he said, from AI Labs to robotics including humanoids.

So far, 73 thematic ETFs have launched this year in the U.S., an 87% increase from the 39 launches seen in 2025, according to data from Morningstar. But the boom in new products is also dredging up some uncomfortable memories: The previous peak for thematic ETF launches arrived in 2021, as the COVID-era market mania was reaching its crescendo. 

 
Thematic ETF launches are surging in 2026 
Year                                          Launches 
2020                                          49 
2021                                          90 
2022                                          59 
2023                                          40 
2024                                          25 
2025                                          39 
2026                                          73 
Source: Morningstar data as of Oct. 19, 2026

While broad index funds like the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY continue to dominate the league tables of products with the most assets under management, the growth in the thematic space suggests investors are increasingly fixating on a more specific opportunity set.

Over the past couple of years, AI has become more influential as an economic force. Economists now say aggressive investment in new data centers is largely responsible for a pickup in the pace of GDP growth.

"This is one of the biggest themes in a generation," said Jay Jacobs, U.S. head of equity ETFs at BlackRock, in a phone interview. "If you look at what's driving the markets, AI is up there with GDP growth and interest rates as one of the biggest factors."

BlackRock listed on Wednesday the iShares Future Robotics and Related Technologies Active ETF RBTX, which actively invests in stocks in categories such as humanoids, industrial automatization, autonomous vehicles, and space and defense, according to Jacobs.

"This is really looking out at what the next major development could look like in the artificial-intelligence space," he said. "The next phase is really AI entering the physical world."

It's hardly the first robotics-focused product to launch this year. Indeed, it has been a particularly popular theme, according to Aniket Ullal, head of ETF research and analytics at CFRA Research. A handful of products have launched in recent months, including the Tuttle-Rareview Humanoid Robotics ETF HOID, which began trading earlier this month.

"People are trying to disaggregate the AI theme," Ullal told MarketWatch by phone.

AI labs, space, cybersecurity

A bunch of AI-lab ETFs recently arrived to the market, including one centered around OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, which had helped popularize artificial intelligence after it was introduced to the public in late 2022.

Harbor Capital Advisors launched the OpenAI Lab Ecosystem ETF OAIW in August, along with the Anthropic AI Lab Ecosystem ETF ANTW, Meta AI Lab Ecosystem ETF MTAW, the Google DeepMind AI Lab Ecosystem ETF DEPW and SpaceXAI Lab Ecosystem ETF XAIW.

"The ecosystem is built around these frontier-model developers," said Armour. "They're like company-specific AI labs," with the ETFs holding shares of their partners or backers, he said.

As AI is maturing, many investors want to trade more precisely around the winners and losers as they shake out, according to Matthew Tuttle, CEO of Tuttle Capital Management.

For example, he pointed to the Roundhill Memory ETF, which launched in early April, as "a perfect product at the perfect time," during a phone interview with MarketWatch. The fund was the first ETF to focus on high-bandwidth memory stocks, providing exposure to the "biggest of the bottleneck trades" in AI, including shares of South Korean companies that U.S. investors couldn't easily buy at the time, he said. "Now what you're seeing, everyone is trying to come up with the next DRAM," said Tuttle, referring to the ETF's ticker.

Since then, he has launched other products offering exposure to the ongoing data-center buildout. In May, his firm launched the Tuttle Capital Pure Play Photonics ETF FOTO, which provides exposure to stocks involved in using laser light in optical fiber instead of copper wire for AI data centers. That same month saw the listing of the Corgi Lithography & Semiconductor Photonics ETF EUV, which Morningstar categorizes under the AI and Big Data theme.

Corgi has launched a flurry of ETF products this year, including a number of thematic funds, like the Corgi Robots & Humanoids ETF CBOT, Corgi Space & Satellite Communications ETF DIPR, Corgi Data & Surveillance ETF EYES, and Corgi AI Cybersecurity ETF XA, according to Morningstar data. Space, another popular theme, has been supercharged by the IPO of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June.

Cybersecurity has also been a big theme, as frontier AI models have seen their capabilities quickly advance. A few high-profile incidents where autonomous AI agents broke out of their sandboxes and infiltrated third-party systems have helped to underscore its importance.

The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF CIBR, which launched in 2015, is currently the biggest cybersecurity product in ETF land. It had $17 billion under management at the end of September, according to Morningstar data.

The AI trade's volatile October

It's been a rocky October for the AI trade as investors question the return on investment from companies doing a heavy amount of spending and borrowing relating to AI to support the buildout of the technology's infrastructure. Still, AI-related stocks have broadly seen big 2026 gains.

Among ETFs that invest in the broad theme, the iShares A. I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF BAI is up more than 21% in 2026 despite tumbling more than 14% this month through Friday. Similarly, the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF AIQ has jumped more than 22% so far this year, although the fund had a much smaller October loss, of more than 4% through Friday, according to FactSet data.

AI is attracting heightened focus lately, after SpaceX (SPCX) reported third-quarter earnings on Oct. 20, and Facebook parent Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) each released quarterly results the following day. Next week brings highly anticipated results from other Big Tech companies involved in AI, including Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG).

With investors now getting access to many different funds with more precise exposures to AI, it's important to remember amid excitement over the transformative technology that "price matters" when identifying investing opportunities in the stock market, Armour cautioned.

"There's so much projection in valuing AI companies," he said, "that it makes it really hard to know whether you're still coming in before the full wave or if you're buying in on the crest."

Bull market for stocks

That S&P 500's strong run in 2026 and in each of the past three years appears to have set the stage for this year's jump in thematic ETFs, as investors sift through ways to sharpen their investing approach in the current bull market for U.S. stocks. The previous thematic ETF boom in 2021 - which Armour said was fueled in part by strategies around environmental, social and governance criteria known as ESG that included clean energy - also coincided with a strong bull market.

In 2021, the S&P 500 SPX booked its third consecutive year of double-digit percentage gains, before slumping 19.4% in 2022 to book its worst performance since 2008, according to FactSet data. The pace of thematic ETF launches fell off significantly in 2022.

AI has been a significant tailwind for the market this year, despite some concern over higher financing costs following a jump in bond yields and as many investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again by year's end. The Fed had been raising rates aggressively in 2022, the year the U.S. stock market slumped, in an effort to battle soaring inflation.

Today, inflation remains elevated, albeit well below levels seen in 2022, prompting the Fed to hike its policy rate in September. The S&P 500 has climbed 11.4% this year through Friday, ending 2.5% below its record closing high booked Oct. 6, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

"When the stock market is particularly strong, then thematic funds tend to follow," said Armour. "When everything seems to be working, it's a lot easier to take on risk."

-Christine Idzelis

data.title: Moderna's cancer vaccine is 'likely' to get approved. Skeptics question if it will be the best option.
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

The first Phase 3 data for a custom cancer vaccine has raised questions about whether the potential new treatment is needed

Moderna's stock was down slightly Friday, after plunging 17.6% on Thursday.

Moderna and Merck proved their custom cancer vaccine cut the risk of melanoma returning for longer than the cancer drug Keytruda, but it may take several years to understand if a therapeutic vaccine is better at beating the disease than immunotherapies.

The companies on Thursday released the highly anticipated Phase 3 data for intismeran, showing that a combination of the experimental vaccine and Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of the cancer returning or the patient passing away by 42% after about two years compared to patients only taking Keytruda.

Though a seemingly striking outcome, the vaccine wasn't as efficacious as some investors had hoped. But the real test of intismeran will be how well the vaccine keeps cancer at bay over time. If it's successful, the custom treatment could radically change how certain patients with cancer are treated.

For now, however, the reaction to the data has been mixed. The study's results were unexpectedly released two days early as a result of a broken embargo, sending down the shares of both companies. Moderna's stock (MRNA) plummeted by as much as 25% on Thursday afternoon to close 17.6% lower. Merck's shares (MRK) closed 1.7% lower.

On Friday, Moderna's stock slipped 1.3%, as did Merck's shares.

Analysts speculated that the haphazard way that the Phase 3 results came out may have rattled investors. Some investors are also asking whether a brand-new technology like intismeran is as game-changing as it's promised to be, especially when compared to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which is the practice of giving Keytruda and other immunotherapies to patients before they go through surgery to have their tumors removed.

"While approval seems likely, commercial success is far less certain," RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh told investors on Thursday. "The data raises fundamental questions about [intismeran's] value proposition relative to standards of care, particularly neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which produces similar efficacy at potentially much less cost."

Keytruda is often given to patients after surgery to prevent the return of their cancer, but sometimes it's administered to patients in advance of surgery to shrink the tumor.

A study published in 2023 found that giving Keytruda to patients with melanoma before surgery significantly extended how long they lived until the cancer came back or spread, or until the patient died, compared to those who received it after surgery. A Phase 3 trial of Yervoy and Opdivo, both of which are immunotherapies owned by Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY), had a similar outcome when given to patients with late-stage melanoma before surgery.

Both studies, however, were done in patients with clinically detectable Stage 3 cancer. That's how the doctors knew to administer the treatment before surgery. But the patients enrolled in the intismeran trial didn't know what stage of cancer they had until after they had surgery, according to Daniel Olson, an oncologist in the UChicago Medicine hospital system, which is one of the sites for other intismeran studies.

"People are saying, 'What's the value of an mRNA vaccine if you can just give [Keytruda] neoadjuvantly?'" he said. "Well, these patients, you can't."

Other analysts also questioned whether comparing studies with different patient populations is fair game.

"While we're not sure this is the right comparison, we see signs [intismeran and Keytruda] have a more durable effect," Jefferies analysts wrote in a note on Friday.

That's the big hope for intismeran, which is a therapeutic vaccine. Experts believe that the protective qualities that we associate with vaccines will work in cancer, hopefully creating lasting stretches of time before cancer comes back than what the currently available drugs can offer.

Intismeran works by training a patient's immune system to respond to the neoantigens in their tumor and then attack any residual cancer cells, according to Jane Healy, Merck's head of oncology early clinical development who ran the Phase 1 study for intismeran.

She believes that's why there was no difference between the patients who got the vaccine and those who got Keytruda in the first six months of the Phase 3 study. It takes time for the immune system to be trained, and for Healy, that means the benefits of a therapeutic vaccine will come later.

"It lends to the durability that [Keytruda] is going in and activating the immune system," she said in an interview. "But [intismeran] is training the immune system in what to recognize."

In the Phase 2 study for the vaccine, the hazard ratio - an important metric for understanding how well a new treatment performs compared to another drug or placebo - was 0.56 after about two years. But the most up-to-date data shows that the hazard ratio didn't degrade much over time, which commonly happens after experimental therapies move from smaller Phase 2 trials into larger Phase 3 studies. It was 0.51 after five years.

"The longer-term data from the Phase 2 - the five years - showing durable responses in these patients out to five years makes me hopeful that this new class of therapies is capable of this durable benefit," Healy said, later adding: "I'm hopeful that we're going to finally see that long-term benefit of vaccines that we get in infectious disease playing out in the oncology setting."

-Jaimy Lee

data.title: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and invest the proceeds. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters'

"We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm 67, my husband is 69, and we've been married 38 years. We've lived in the same four-bedroom colonial for 32 of those years. It's paid off and worth $1.5 million. We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security and a small pension from his old job. No debt, and our kids are on their own.

So this isn't a money problem, but we can't talk about retirement anymore without it turning into a fight. He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters, and invest the rest. He has a spreadsheet. I've seen it open on the laptop at the kitchen table at 11 p.m., with property taxes, insurance and the lawn guy all in little columns.

He says we're heating rooms nobody uses, and he's right that nobody has slept in the fourth bedroom since our youngest left 12 years ago. It holds a treadmill (of course) and about nine boxes of Christmas decorations. He's also right that the place is a money pit. The roof has maybe three years left and the furnace sounds like it's clearing its throat every morning.

Last spring, we dropped $18,000 on a sewer line. Every time something breaks, Ron looks at me across the room like the case is closed. But the pantry door has pencil marks on it, one for every kid every year, with the dates in my handwriting. We brought both babies home to this house. He calls it sentimental clutter. I thought that was mean.

He slipped on the back steps last winter, and we both pretended it didn't scare us, but he could have just as easily slipped on another stairwell. All three kids live within an hour away. We host Thanksgiving every year, 14 people if everyone shows up, and the grandkids spend half of it out in the yard. Our daughter said she'd be sad if we sold.

I worry a small kitchen means the end of Thanksgiving, and that the grandkids will come less often if there's no yard. Ron says I'm inventing reasons because I'm scared of change. Maybe I am. But I don't want to be 75 and regret that we gave it up too soon. How do we decide whether staying is worth what it costs? Is it foolish to keep a house this big?

A Sentimental 67-Year-Old Homeowner

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I am a pretty cautious person': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

Dear Sentimental,

Take the pantry door with you when you go.

Joking aside, I think that's an idea worth exploring. Take whatever has sentimental value to your new home. If you live in a large, drafty house that costs money to heat, costs you thousands of dollars a year in property taxes and insurance, and you're only using a small number of rooms, it may no longer make financial sense to stay. But plenty of people live in the house where they raised their family because they love the house, the garden, and the feeling they get when they close the front door behind them. That's worth a lot.

It's as much a "money problem" as it is an everything-else problem. You have Social Security, which I'll assume is $4,000 a month between the two of you. If you follow the 4% rule and withdraw from your $1.8 million in savings in the first year, that would give you $72,000 before taxes. Whether your savings could endure that level of withdrawals over the rest of your lives depends on how much you spend, how you invest your nest egg, what happens in the stock market, how much you get in Social Security, and your husband's pension.

Your retirement fund could last until you're in your 90s, or for another 30 years (to be gloriously optimistic). An $80,000 income from $1.8 million equates to a 4.44% withdrawal rate in the first year, while an initial 4% withdrawal, adjusted for inflation in subsequent years, would give you $72,000 in the first year. You know your own lifestyle best, but this should give you a pretty good idea if you will need to downsize later. If you sold your house for $1.5 million and bought another for half the price, that would be a nice profit. You can afford to stay. You have choices.

There's plenty of room for discussion between his computer spreadsheet and your very real love for this place you call home. For starters, a lot of thought and time probably went into that spreadsheet. It may be his way of trying to make the next stage of your lives more secure. If you ended up with $2.7 million in investable assets after selling your home and buying another, a 4% initial withdrawal would - or could - give you an income of $108,000 a year before taxes. Would that difference affect how you want to live in retirement?

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire, yet she wants to take an $8,000 trip to Italy. We have $4 million. Do I keep working?

A trial move

Moving makes more sense if you believe it would be expensive or impractical to future-proof your current home, with bedrooms and a decent bathroom on the ground floor. The costs of maintaining the house and your ability to live there safely as you age all matter. I agree with both of you that $18,000 for a sewer line is a lot of money, and that money could have been spent on a golf-club membership or several trips to Europe or South America. I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

What's the point of moving if one of you is unhappy? It's hard to imagine handing your home over to another couple or family and settling into a smaller space. If you talk to anyone who has lived in several properties throughout their life, they will probably have one home they still think about fondly. But it's "our" belongings - clothing, artwork, knickknacks, and all the stuff we accumulate (and get rid of as the years progress) - that create and, yes, recreate that familiar space that feels like home.

Explore your options with the help of a financial adviser, a couples therapist, or both. The former can help you compare the costs of staying versus going, while the latter can help you see each other's viewpoints. Once you have more clarity, an open discussion with your children could also help - not to get their approval, but to get their perspective. They know your family dynamics well and may have ideas. The starting point is that there is no "he's right and I'm wrong" or "I'm wrong and he's actually right." You both have valid points.

Rather than renting out your home or having strangers live among your belongings, why not spend some time in a rental property that could substitute as a long-term home. Visit open houses and imagine your life outside of this house, including during Thanksgiving and visits from your grandkids. It wouldn't hurt to have a survey done on your home to see how much you might have to pay for upgrades. You and your husband are not on opposing sides. You're on the same side. Just because he wants to downsize does not mean that he doesn't love the memories, too.
